whyWrongByChoice.C: Cardiac catheterization is invasive, time-consuming, and not the appropriate first-line diagnostic tool for aortic dissection, especially in a hemodynamically unstable patient.
whyWrongByChoice.D: MR angiography, while accurate, is time-consuming and requires transport to the MRI suite, making it impractical and potentially dangerous for a hemodynamically unstable patient.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man with a history of hypertension and smoking is diagnosed with a Stanford type A aortic dissection on CT angiography. He is hemodynamically stable. The surgical team is consulted. Which of the following is the most appropriate definitive management for this patient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Medical management with intravenous beta-blockers and intensive care unit monitoring alone

choices.label: B
choices.text: Medical management with an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor to lower blood pressure

choices.label: C
choices.text: Immediate surgical repair of the aorta with postoperative blood pressure management

choices.label: D
choices.text: Endovascular stent placement across the dissection with medical blood pressure control

choices.label: E
choices.text: Observation with serial CT angiography and elective surgical repair if the dissection progresses

explanation.summary: All Stanford type A aortic dissections require immediate surgical repair, regardless of hemodynamic stability, due to the high risk of life-threatening complications including cardiac tamponade and aortic rupture.
explanation.whyCorrect: All Stanford type A aortic dissections merit immediate surgical treatment to repair the aorta. Type A dissections are more dangerous because they can spread to the heart, causing hemopericardium, cardiac tamponade, coronary artery occlusion, or acute aortic regurgitation. Medical management alone is reserved for uncomplicated type B dissections.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Medical management alone with beta-blockers is appropriate for uncomplicated Stanford type B dissections, not type A; all type A dissections require immediate surgical intervention.
whyWrongByChoice.B: ACE inhibitors are not the preferred first-line antihypertensive for aortic dissection (beta-blockers are preferred), and medical management alone is inadequate for type A dissections.
whyWrongByChoice.D: While endovascular techniques may be used for some complicated type B dissections, Stanford type A dissections require open surgical repair due to the involvement of the ascending aorta and associated cardiac structures.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Observation with serial imaging is appropriate for small, asymptomatic aortic aneurysms, not acute type A aortic dissections, which are surgical emergencies with high mortality if untreated.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman with a known history of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome presents to the emergency department with sudden onset of severe interscapular pain. CT angiography reveals an aortic dissection limited to the descending thoracic aorta. A biopsy of the aortic wall would most likely reveal which of the following histopathologic findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Dense neutrophilic infiltration with microabscess formation within the tunica intima

choices.label: B
choices.text: Smooth muscle cell dropout, elastic tissue fragmentation, and proteoglycan-rich extracellular matrix accumulation in the tunica media

choices.label: C
choices.text: Transmural granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells in all three vessel layers

choices.label: D
choices.text: Fibrointimal proliferation with marked neovascularization of the tunica adventitia

choices.label: E
choices.text: Lipid-laden macrophage accumulation forming a large necrotic core beneath the tunica intima

explanation.summary: Cystic medial degeneration is the histologic lesion most frequently detected in cases of aortic dissection, particularly in patients with connective tissue diseases such as Ehlers-Danlos syndrome. It is characterized by smooth muscle cell dropout, elastic tissue fragmentation, and proteoglycan-rich extracellular matrix accumulation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cystic medial degeneration (CMD) is the histologic lesion most frequently detected in aortic dissection. It is characterized by smooth muscle cell dropout and necrosis, elastic tissue fragmentation, and accumulations of amorphous proteoglycan-rich extracellular matrix. CMD is commonly associated with connective tissue diseases such as Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and Marfan syndrome.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Neutrophilic infiltration and microabscesses are characteristic of infectious aortitis (mycotic aneurysm), not the degenerative changes seen in connective tissue disease-related dissections.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Transmural granulomatous inflammation with giant cells is seen in giant cell arteritis or Takayasu arteritis, not in Ehlers-Danlos syndrome-related aortic dissection.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Fibrointimal proliferation with neovascularization is seen in chronic vasculopathies and transplant vasculopathy, not in the acute degenerative changes of aortic dissection.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Lipid-laden macrophage accumulation forming a necrotic core is characteristic of advanced atherosclerotic plaques, which primarily involve the tunica intima, not the medial degeneration seen in dissection.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with chronic hypertension presents to the emergency department with severe tearing back pain. CT angiography confirms a Stanford type B aortic dissection without evidence of organ ischemia. He is admitted to the ICU and started on intravenous labetalol. Which of the following target values for blood pressure and heart rate are most appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Blood pressure less than 120/80 mm Hg with heart rate less than 60 bpm

choices.label: B
choices.text: Blood pressure less than 140/90 mm Hg with heart rate less than 80 bpm

choices.label: C
choices.text: Blood pressure less than 160/100 mm Hg with heart rate less than 100 bpm

choices.label: D
choices.text: Blood pressure less than 100/60 mm Hg with heart rate less than 50 bpm

choices.label: E
choices.text: Blood pressure less than 130/85 mm Hg with heart rate less than 70 bpm

explanation.summary: In medical management of Stanford type B aortic dissection, the target blood pressure is less than 120/80 mm Hg with pulse rates less than 60 bpm to minimize shear forces on the intimal tear.
explanation.whyCorrect: For Stanford type B dissections managed medically, beta-blockers and antihypertensives are used to reduce shear forces on the intimal tear. The specific targets stated in the source material are a blood pressure less than 120/80 mm Hg and pulse rates less than 60 bpm.

whyWrongByChoice.B: While closer to the target, a blood pressure of 140/90 mm Hg and heart rate of 80 bpm are both above the recommended targets of less than 120/80 mm Hg and less than 60 bpm.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A target of 160/100 mm Hg is far too high for aortic dissection management; ongoing hypertension at this level would continue to exert excessive shear force on the intimal tear.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A target of less than 100/60 mm Hg and less than 50 bpm is overly aggressive and could lead to hypotension and end-organ hypoperfusion; the recommended targets are less than 120/80 mm Hg and less than 60 bpm.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A blood pressure target of 130/85 mm Hg and heart rate of 70 bpm are both above the recommended goals for aortic dissection management.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man presents with acute severe chest pain radiating to his back. CT angiography reveals a Stanford type A aortic dissection. While in the emergency department, he develops acute onset of severe epigastric pain and bloody diarrhea. Serum lactate is markedly elevated. Which of the following complications of aortic dissection best explains his new gastrointestinal symptoms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Stress-related gastric ulceration from the acute dissection pain and catecholamine surge

choices.label: B
choices.text: Occlusion of the mesenteric arteries by the dissection flap or false lumen hematoma

choices.label: C
choices.text: Rupture of the dissection into the peritoneal cavity with hemoperitoneum

choices.label: D
choices.text: Medication-induced gastrointestinal bleeding from intravenous antihypertensive agents

choices.label: E
choices.text: Acute pancreatitis triggered by hypoperfusion of the celiac trunk from the dissection

explanation.summary: Aortic dissection can occlude branch vessels including mesenteric arteries through extension of the intimal flap or compression by the false lumen hematoma, leading to mesenteric ischemia with abdominal pain, bloody diarrhea, and elevated lactate.
explanation.whyCorrect: The intimal flap created by the dissection may extend into branching vessels and occlude the lumen, or the hematoma within the false lumen can compress the openings of the mesenteric arteries. This blockage leads to mesenteric ischemia, which presents with severe abdominal pain, bloody diarrhea, and markedly elevated serum lactate from end-organ ischemia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Stress ulceration typically occurs in critically ill patients over days and would not explain the acute bloody diarrhea with elevated lactate, which indicates mesenteric ischemia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Aortic dissection rupture into the peritoneal cavity would cause hemorrhagic shock rather than the specific presentation of bloody diarrhea with elevated lactate suggesting bowel ischemia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Antihypertensive agents such as beta-blockers do not cause acute gastrointestinal bleeding; the clinical picture of bloody diarrhea with elevated lactate in the setting of aortic dissection points to mesenteric ischemia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: While celiac trunk involvement could theoretically contribute to pancreatitis, the presentation of bloody diarrhea with elevated lactate is more consistent with mesenteric ischemia from mesenteric artery occlusion.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man with poorly controlled hypertension presents with sudden onset of severe tearing chest pain. On physical examination, his right pupil is constricted, his right eyelid is drooping, and the right side of his face is not sweating. CT angiography confirms a Stanford type A aortic dissection. Which of the following structures is most likely being compressed by the dissecting aorta to produce these findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Superior cervical sympathetic ganglion by the expanding aorta

choices.label: B
choices.text: Right vagus nerve as it descends along the tracheoesophageal groove

choices.label: C
choices.text: Right recurrent laryngeal nerve as it loops around the aortic arch

choices.label: D
choices.text: Right phrenic nerve as it crosses the anterior surface of the heart

choices.label: E
choices.text: Stellate ganglion at the level of the first rib and subclavian artery

explanation.summary: The triad of ptosis, miosis, and anhidrosis (Horner syndrome) results from compression of the superior cervical sympathetic ganglion by the expanding aortic dissection.
explanation.whyCorrect: The enlarging aortic dissection can compress adjacent structures, including the superior cervical sympathetic nerve ganglia, leading to Horner syndrome. This presents as the classic triad of ptosis (drooping eyelid), miosis (constricted pupil), and anhidrosis (lack of sweating of the face) on the ipsilateral side.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Vagus nerve compression would cause autonomic and gastrointestinal symptoms such as bradycardia or voice changes, not the specific sympathetic denervation pattern of Horner syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Compression of the recurrent laryngeal nerve by the aorta causes hoarseness, not the triad of ptosis, miosis, and anhidrosis described in this case.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Phrenic nerve compression would cause diaphragmatic paralysis with dyspnea and an elevated hemidiaphragm on chest X-ray, not the oculosympathetic findings of Horner syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: While the stellate ganglion is part of the sympathetic chain, the source material specifically identifies compression of the superior cervical sympathetic nerve ganglia as the mechanism for Horner syndrome in aortic dissection.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man with a history of bicuspid aortic valve is brought to the emergency department after a motor vehicle collision. He complains of sudden severe tearing chest pain. CT angiography reveals an intimal flap in the ascending aorta with a false lumen containing hematoma. The pathologic process in this patient's aorta involves blood accumulating in which of the following anatomic layers?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Between the tunica intima and the internal elastic lamina

choices.label: B
choices.text: Within the tunica adventitia between the connective tissue fibers

choices.label: C
choices.text: Within the lumen of the aorta forming a mural thrombus along the intimal surface

choices.label: D
choices.text: Within the tunica media after entry through a tear in the tunica intima

choices.label: E
choices.text: In the pericardial space between the visceral and parietal pericardium

explanation.summary: In aortic dissection, blood enters the vessel wall through a tear in the tunica intima and accumulates within the tunica media, creating a false lumen that separates the layers of smooth muscle.
explanation.whyCorrect: A tear in the tunica intima allows blood to enter the vessel wall and collect within the tunica media, where it 'unzips' the layers of smooth muscle down the length of the vessel, creating a false lumen. The hematoma is contained only by the outer tunica adventitia. This is the fundamental pathologic process of aortic dissection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: While the tear occurs at the level of the intima, the blood does not simply collect between the intima and internal elastic lamina; it tracks into the tunica media, dissecting between its smooth muscle layers.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Blood does not accumulate within the tunica adventitia in aortic dissection; the adventitia serves as the outer containment layer preventing complete rupture. If blood breaches the adventitia, frank aortic rupture occurs.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mural thrombus formation along the intimal surface occurs within the lumen of aortic aneurysms, not within the vessel wall; in dissection, blood is within the vessel wall itself, not the lumen.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Blood in the pericardial space (hemopericardium) is a complication of aortic dissection rupture, not the location of the primary pathologic process of dissection itself.

questions.stem: A 56-year-old man with Stanford type A aortic dissection undergoes emergent surgical repair. Postoperatively, his surgeon discusses risk factors for aortic dissection with the medical team. Which of the following statements regarding the epidemiology and risk factors of aortic dissection is most accurate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The incidence of aortic dissection is approximately 20 per 100,000 patients annually, making it more common than aortic aneurysm

choices.label: B
choices.text: Young patients with aortic dissection most commonly have poorly controlled essential hypertension as the underlying cause

choices.label: C
choices.text: Female sex is the strongest demographic risk factor for the development of aortic dissection

choices.label: D
choices.text: Aortic dissection most commonly affects younger women aged 30 to 50 years with autoimmune conditions

choices.label: E
choices.text: The incidence of aortic dissection is 2 to 3 per 100,000 patients, and younger patients most often have a congenital disorder of collagen

explanation.summary: The incidence of aortic dissection is 2 to 3 per 100,000 patients (about half that of aortic aneurysm). In younger patients, the cause is most often a congenital disorder of collagen, while older patients typically have hypertension-related disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: The incidence of aortic dissections is 2 to 3 per 100,000 patients, about half that of aortic aneurysm. Younger patients with aortic dissection most often have a congenital disorder of collagen (such as Marfan or Ehlers-Danlos syndrome) with defects in elastin and collagen synthesis, while older patients typically have disease caused by severe, poorly controlled hypertension.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The incidence of aortic dissection is 2 to 3 per 100,000 patients, which is about half that of aortic aneurysm, not more common than it.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Young patients with aortic dissection most commonly have congenital connective tissue disorders (e.g., Marfan or Ehlers-Danlos syndrome), not essential hypertension, which is the primary cause in older patients.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Male sex, not female sex, is a risk factor for aortic dissection; it is most common in older males aged 60 to 80 years.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Aortic dissection most commonly affects older males aged 60 to 80 years, not younger women; autoimmune conditions are not the most common underlying cause.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man presents with a 3-month history of recurrent sinusitis, bloody nasal discharge, and a 2-week history of hemoptysis. Physical examination reveals a saddle nose deformity and scattered bilateral lung crackles. Urinalysis shows hematuria and red blood cell casts. Serum creatinine is elevated. Laboratory testing reveals a positive c-ANCA with anti-PR3 antibodies. A lung biopsy is performed. Which of the following histopathologic findings is most characteristic of this patient's condition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Diffuse eosinophilic infiltration with Charcot-Leyden crystals

choices.label: B
choices.text: IgA immune complex deposition in vessel walls with fibrin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Necrotizing granulomas with necrotizing or granulomatous vasculitis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Noncaseating granulomas with asteroid bodies in giant cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transmural fibrinoid necrosis without granuloma formation

explanation.summary: This patient has granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA), evidenced by the classic triad of upper respiratory tract disease (sinusitis, saddle nose, bloody nasal discharge), lung involvement (hemoptysis), and renal disease (hematuria, RBC casts), with positive c-ANCA/anti-PR3. The histologic hallmark is necrotizing granulomas with necrotizing or granulomatous vasculitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: GPA is histologically characterized by a triad: necrotizing granulomas along the respiratory tract, necrotizing or granulomatous vasculitis (most prominent in lungs and upper airways), and focal necrotizing crescentic glomerulonephritis. Necrotizing granulomas are the histologic hallmark.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Diffuse eosinophilic infiltration is characteristic of EGPA (Churg-Strauss syndrome), which presents with asthma and allergic symptoms, not saddle nose deformity and c-ANCA positivity.
whyWrongByChoice.B: IgA immune complex deposition is the pathologic finding in IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein purpura), an immune complex-mediated small-vessel vasculitis rather than an ANCA-associated vasculitis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Noncaseating granulomas with asteroid bodies are characteristic of sarcoidosis, not GPA. GPA granulomas are necrotizing, whereas sarcoid granulomas are noncaseating.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Transmural fibrinoid necrosis without granuloma formation is characteristic of polyarteritis nodosa (PAN), a medium-vessel vasculitis that is ANCA-negative and spares the lungs.

questions.stem: A 43-year-old woman with a 15-year history of asthma presents with worsening dyspnea, a new purpuric rash on her lower extremities, and intermittent abdominal pain with bloody stools over the past 6 weeks. She also reports unintentional weight loss, night sweats, and nasal congestion with polyps. Laboratory studies show a white blood cell count of 14,000/μL with 22% eosinophils. A chest radiograph demonstrates bilateral streaky infiltrates. Which of the following serologic markers is most likely to be positive in this patient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies

choices.label: B
choices.text: Anti-proteinase 3 antibodies with cytoplasmic staining pattern

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cryoglobulins precipitating at temperatures below 37°C

choices.label: D
choices.text: Anti-myeloperoxidase antibodies with perinuclear staining pattern

choices.label: E
choices.text: Anti-double-stranded DNA antibodies with homogeneous ANA pattern

explanation.summary: This patient has eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA), evidenced by longstanding asthma, nasal polyps, marked peripheral eosinophilia, GI involvement, and pulmonary infiltrates. Approximately 50% of EGPA cases are associated with MPO-ANCA (p-ANCA), which has anti-myeloperoxidase antibodies with a perinuclear staining pattern.
explanation.whyCorrect: EGPA is associated with MPO-ANCA in approximately 50% of cases. Anti-MPO antibodies produce a perinuclear staining pattern (p-ANCA), distinguishing them from the cytoplasmic pattern (c-ANCA) seen with anti-PR3 antibodies in GPA.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anti-GBM antibodies are found in anti-glomerular basement membrane disease (formerly Goodpasture syndrome), which presents with pulmonary-renal syndrome but without asthma, eosinophilia, or nasal polyps.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Anti-PR3 antibodies with c-ANCA pattern are characteristic of granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA), which presents with sinusitis, saddle nose deformity, and necrotizing granulomas, not asthma and eosinophilia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cryoglobulins are associated with cryoglobulinemic vasculitis, which is most commonly caused by hepatitis C infection and does not present with asthma or peripheral eosinophilia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Anti-dsDNA antibodies are characteristic of systemic lupus erythematosus, which has different clinical features and does not cause peripheral eosinophilia or asthma.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy is brought to the pediatrician with a 3-day history of a raised purple rash on his buttocks and lower extremities. His mother reports that he had an upper respiratory infection 10 days ago. He now complains of abdominal pain and knee pain. Urinalysis reveals microscopic hematuria. A complete blood count is within normal limits. Which of the following pathophysiologic mechanisms is most directly responsible for this patient's clinical presentation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Activation of neutrophils by anti-proteinase 3 antibodies targeting endothelial cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Autoantibodies directed against collagen in the glomerular and alveolar basement membranes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cryoglobulin precipitation in small vessels triggered by cold temperature exposure

choices.label: D
choices.text: Deposition of IgA immune complexes in small blood vessels causing inflammation and extravasation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Myeloperoxidase antibody-mediated neutrophil degranulation with small-vessel necrotizing vasculitis

explanation.summary: This child presents with IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein purpura): palpable purpura on buttocks and lower extremities following a URI, with abdominal pain, arthritis, and hematuria. The pathophysiology involves deposition of IgA immune complexes, fibrin, and complement in small blood vessels, causing inflammation and blood extravasation.
explanation.whyCorrect: IgA vasculitis is an immune complex-mediated disease involving deposition of IgA immune complexes, fibrin, and complement components in small blood vessels. This leads to inflammation that damages vessels and causes blood extravasation, clinically manifesting as purpura.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anti-PR3 antibodies (c-ANCA) activating neutrophils is the mechanism of granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA), which presents with upper and lower respiratory tract disease, not purpura with abdominal pain in a child.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Autoantibodies against basement membrane collagen is the mechanism of anti-GBM disease (Goodpasture syndrome), which presents with pulmonary hemorrhage and rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, not purpura.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cryoglobulin precipitation is the mechanism of cryoglobulinemic vasculitis, which is most commonly associated with hepatitis C infection and presents differently from this child's clinical picture.
whyWrongByChoice.E: MPO antibody-mediated neutrophil degranulation is the mechanism in microscopic polyangiitis, which presents with hemoptysis and nephritic syndrome, not gravity-dependent purpura in a child following URI.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man presents with a 2-week history of hemoptysis and dark-colored urine. He reports progressive fatigue and bilateral lower extremity edema. Physical examination reveals bilateral lung crackles and pitting edema. Laboratory studies show serum creatinine of 4.2 mg/dL (baseline 1.0 mg/dL), hematuria with red blood cell casts, and proteinuria. A chest radiograph shows bilateral alveolar infiltrates. Serologic testing reveals positive p-ANCA and anti-MPO antibodies. c-ANCA is negative. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Anti-glomerular basement membrane disease

choices.label: B
choices.text: Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis

choices.label: D
choices.text: IgA vasculitis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Microscopic polyangiitis

explanation.summary: This patient presents with a pulmonary-renal syndrome (hemoptysis with rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis) and positive p-ANCA with anti-MPO antibodies. This combination is most consistent with microscopic polyangiitis (MPA), where the classically associated antibody is p-ANCA reacting with myeloperoxidase.
explanation.whyCorrect: MPA can present with hemoptysis secondary to diffuse alveolar hemorrhage and nephritic syndrome with hematuria. The classically associated antibody is p-ANCA/anti-MPO. In the setting of combined lung and renal disease, a positive p-ANCA is strongly suggestive of MPA.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anti-GBM disease also presents with pulmonary-renal syndrome but is diagnosed by detecting anti-GBM antibodies, not p-ANCA/anti-MPO antibodies. It is treated with plasma exchange.
whyWrongByChoice.B: EGPA can be associated with p-ANCA, but it characteristically presents with asthma, allergic rhinitis, nasal polyps, and peripheral eosinophilia, none of which are present in this patient.
whyWrongByChoice.C: GPA is associated with c-ANCA and anti-PR3 antibodies, not p-ANCA/anti-MPO. GPA also characteristically involves the upper respiratory tract with sinusitis and saddle nose deformity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: IgA vasculitis is an immune complex-mediated vasculitis that is ANCA-negative and most common in children, presenting with purpura, abdominal pain, and arthritis.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old woman with a 20-year history of chronic hepatitis C presents with fatigue, arthralgias, and a new purpuric rash on her lower extremities. She also reports numbness and tingling in her feet. Laboratory studies reveal elevated serum creatinine, positive rheumatoid factor, and decreased complement levels. A specific serum test reveals antibodies that precipitate out of solution when the temperature is lowered below body temperature. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment approach?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antiviral therapy targeting the underlying hepatitis C infection

choices.label: B
choices.text: High-dose intravenous methylprednisolone pulse therapy alone

choices.label: C
choices.text: Immediate plasma exchange followed by cyclophosphamide

choices.label: D
choices.text: Intravenous immunoglobulin and high-dose aspirin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Mepolizumab targeting interleukin-5 to reduce inflammation

explanation.summary: This patient has cryoglobulinemic vasculitis secondary to chronic hepatitis C. Cryoglobulins are antibodies that precipitate at temperatures below body temperature. The goal of treatment is to address the underlying cause, which in this case is antiviral therapy for hepatitis C.
explanation.whyCorrect: The primary treatment approach for cryoglobulinemia is to address the underlying cause. Since hepatitis C is the most common cause, and this patient has chronic HCV infection, antiviral therapy targeting HCV is the most appropriate initial treatment.

whyWrongByChoice.B: While corticosteroids may be needed for patients with severe vasculitis, the primary approach is treating the underlying cause. Pulse steroids alone do not address the hepatitis C driving the cryoglobulin formation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Plasma exchange is reserved for anti-GBM disease and severe refractory vasculitis. The initial approach in HCV-associated cryoglobulinemia is antiviral therapy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: IVIG and high-dose aspirin is the treatment for Kawasaki disease, a medium-vessel vasculitis in children, not for cryoglobulinemic vasculitis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Mepolizumab is an IL-5 blocking antibody approved for treatment of EGPA, not cryoglobulinemic vasculitis.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man presents to the emergency department with acute hemoptysis and progressive dyspnea over the past 5 days. He also reports dark-colored urine and decreased urine output. Serum creatinine is 5.1 mg/dL. Urinalysis shows red blood cell casts. A chest radiograph demonstrates bilateral diffuse alveolar infiltrates. Serologic testing reveals circulating antibodies directed against a specific collagen epitope. ANCA testing is negative. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for this patient's condition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Corticosteroids combined with cyclophosphamide or rituximab

choices.label: B
choices.text: High-dose aspirin with intravenous immunoglobulin infusion

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mepolizumab targeting interleukin-5 with low-dose prednisone

choices.label: D
choices.text: Plasma exchange to remove pathogenic circulating antibodies

choices.label: E
choices.text: Supportive care only as the condition is self-limiting

explanation.summary: This patient has anti-GBM disease (formerly Goodpasture syndrome), presenting with pulmonary hemorrhage and rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis. Anti-GBM antibodies target collagen epitopes in the glomerular and alveolar basement membranes. ANCA is negative. Treatment is plasma exchange to remove the pathogenic anti-GBM antibodies.
explanation.whyCorrect: Anti-GBM disease is diagnosed by detecting anti-GBM antibodies in the serum and is treated with plasma exchange to remove the pathogenic circulating antibodies targeting glomerular and alveolar basement membrane collagen.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Corticosteroids with cyclophosphamide or rituximab is the treatment regimen for ANCA-associated vasculitides (GPA, EGPA, MPA), not anti-GBM disease. This patient is ANCA-negative.
whyWrongByChoice.B: IVIG and high-dose aspirin is the treatment for Kawasaki disease in children, not for anti-GBM disease in adults with pulmonary-renal syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mepolizumab is an IL-5 inhibitor approved for EGPA, which presents with asthma and eosinophilia, not anti-GBM disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Anti-GBM disease is not self-limiting and can be fatal without treatment. IgA vasculitis is the vasculitis that typically resolves spontaneously.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man with a history of asthma and allergic rhinitis presents with progressive dyspnea, unintentional weight loss, and intermittent abdominal pain over the past 3 months. He has also developed numbness in his left foot. Laboratory studies show a WBC count of 16,500/μL with 25% eosinophils. Echocardiography reveals a reduced ejection fraction of 35%. A skin biopsy from a purpuric lesion on his lower leg shows eosinophilic infiltration of the vessel wall. His physician is concerned about the prognosis. Which of the following is the most common cause of death in this patient's condition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cerebral hemorrhage from ruptured intracranial aneurysms

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cardiac involvement

choices.label: C
choices.text: End-stage renal disease from crescentic glomerulonephritis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Massive pulmonary hemorrhage from diffuse alveolar damage

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sepsis from intestinal perforation and bacterial peritonitis

explanation.summary: This patient has EGPA (Churg-Strauss syndrome), evidenced by asthma, eosinophilia, neuropathy, purpura, and reduced ejection fraction. Cardiac involvement is the most serious complication and the main cause of death in EGPA, manifesting as pericarditis, myocardial infarction, and heart failure from myocarditis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cardiac involvement is explicitly identified as the most serious complication and the main cause of death in patients with EGPA. It can manifest as pericarditis, myocardial infarction, and heart failure. This patient's reduced ejection fraction already demonstrates cardiac involvement.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cerebral hemorrhage from intracranial aneurysms is not a characteristic complication of EGPA. Stroke may occur but is not the most common cause of mortality.
whyWrongByChoice.C: While renal involvement with glomerulonephritis can occur in EGPA, end-stage renal disease is not the most common cause of death. Cardiac disease predominates.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Although pulmonary infiltrates occur in EGPA, massive pulmonary hemorrhage is more characteristic of MPA or anti-GBM disease, not EGPA.
whyWrongByChoice.E: While GI involvement including gut ulcerations and perforations can occur in the vasculitic stage of EGPA, cardiac disease remains the leading cause of mortality.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department with a 4-day history of a raised purplish rash on her buttocks and lower extremities, colicky abdominal pain, and swollen knees. She had a sore throat 2 weeks ago that resolved on its own. Urinalysis shows microscopic hematuria with mild proteinuria. Complete blood count is normal. Her pediatrician suspects IgA vasculitis. The parents ask about the expected clinical course. Which of the following is the most accurate statement regarding the prognosis of this condition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Spontaneous recovery typically occurs within 3 to 6 months even without specific therapy

choices.label: B
choices.text: Most patients progress to end-stage renal disease within 6 months without aggressive treatment

choices.label: C
choices.text: Immediate immunosuppressive therapy is required to prevent fatal cardiac complications within weeks

choices.label: D
choices.text: The disease follows a chronic relapsing course requiring lifelong immunosuppressive therapy

choices.label: E
choices.text: The mortality rate exceeds 50% within 5 years regardless of treatment intensity

explanation.summary: IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein purpura) is typically a self-limiting illness with spontaneous recovery after 3 to 6 months, even without therapy. The exception is cases with severe renal disease, where corticosteroids and immunomodulating agents may be needed to prevent permanent glomerular damage.
explanation.whyCorrect: IgA vasculitis is typically a self-limiting illness, with spontaneous recovery occurring within 3 to 6 months even without specific therapy. This distinguishes it from other vasculitides that require aggressive immunosuppression.

whyWrongByChoice.C: IgA vasculitis does not cause fatal cardiac complications. Cardiac involvement is characteristic of EGPA, not IgA vasculitis. IgA vasculitis is self-limiting in most cases.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Most patients do not progress to end-stage renal disease. While severe renal involvement can occur, the vast majority of cases resolve spontaneously.
whyWrongByChoice.D: IgA vasculitis does not follow a chronic relapsing course requiring lifelong therapy. It is self-limiting, though corticosteroids may be used for cases with severe renal involvement.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Survival rates for IgA vasculitis are generally good, with 5-year survival around 75% and 10-year survival around 60%. The mortality rate does not exceed 50% within 5 years.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man presents with a 2-month history of recurrent nosebleeds, progressive hearing loss, and a productive cough occasionally streaked with blood. He has lost 6 kg unintentionally. Physical examination reveals nasal mucosal ulceration and bilateral pulmonary crackles. Urinalysis shows hematuria with red blood cell casts. Serum creatinine is elevated at 3.2 mg/dL. Serologic testing reveals c-ANCA positivity. Both c-ANCA and anti-PR3 antibodies are detected. What is the diagnostic specificity of this combined serologic finding for his underlying condition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Approximately 50%, requiring biopsy for definitive diagnosis in all cases

choices.label: B
choices.text: Approximately 70%, useful only as a screening test before invasive procedures

choices.label: C
choices.text: Approximately 80%, equivalent to the specificity of anti-PR3 antibodies alone

choices.label: D
choices.text: Greater than 90%, reflecting the specificity of c-ANCA testing alone

choices.label: E
choices.text: Greater than 99%, making this combination highly specific for the diagnosis

explanation.summary: This patient has GPA with the classic triad of upper respiratory, pulmonary, and renal involvement. A positive c-ANCA alone is >90% specific for GPA. When both c-ANCA and anti-PR3 antibodies are present together, the diagnostic specificity for GPA exceeds 99%.
explanation.whyCorrect: c-ANCA testing alone has >90% specificity for GPA, and anti-PR3 antibodies are present in 80-95% of ANCA-positive patients. When both c-ANCA and anti-PR3 are present, the diagnostic specificity for GPA exceeds 99%.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A specificity of 50% significantly underestimates the diagnostic value of combined c-ANCA and anti-PR3 testing. This combination is one of the most specific serologic findings in vasculitis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A specificity of 70% undervalues the combined testing. The c-ANCA test alone has specificity greater than 90% for GPA.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Anti-PR3 antibodies alone are present in 80-95% of ANCA-positive GPA patients. The combination with c-ANCA positivity raises specificity above 99%, not merely to 80%.
whyWrongByChoice.D: While c-ANCA alone has >90% specificity, the combination with anti-PR3 pushes specificity even higher, to more than 99%.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old woman with a 10-year history of asthma presents to the clinic reporting progressive nasal congestion over the past year. She has required two polypectomies for nasal polyps in the past 6 months. Over the past 3 weeks, she has developed worsening fatigue, intermittent fevers, night sweats, and diffuse abdominal cramping with occasional bloody stools. Complete blood count reveals a WBC of 18,000/μL with 30% eosinophils. A chest radiograph shows bilateral migratory pulmonary infiltrates. Paranasal sinus CT demonstrates mucosal thickening. Which of the following additional findings would be required to meet the diagnostic criteria for this patient's most likely condition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Blood eosinophil count greater than 10% of total white blood cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies in the serum

choices.label: C
choices.text: Positive c-ANCA with anti-PR3 antibody confirmation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Saddle nose deformity with nasal septal perforation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Serum cryoglobulins with hepatitis C viral RNA detection

explanation.summary: This patient has EGPA (Churg-Strauss syndrome) based on asthma, nasal polyps, eosinophilia, GI involvement, and migratory pulmonary infiltrates. The EGPA diagnostic criteria include asthma, migratory pulmonary infiltrates, paranasal sinus abnormalities, neuropathy, and a blood eosinophil count more than 10%.
explanation.whyCorrect: The EGPA diagnostic criteria include asthma symptoms, migratory pulmonary infiltrates on x-ray, paranasal sinus abnormalities, neuropathy, and a blood eosinophil count more than 10%. This patient already has asthma, pulmonary infiltrates, and sinus disease; eosinophil count >10% is another required criterion that she meets (30%).

whyWrongByChoice.B: Anti-GBM antibodies are diagnostic of anti-GBM disease (Goodpasture syndrome), not EGPA. Anti-GBM disease presents with pulmonary-renal syndrome without asthma or eosinophilia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: c-ANCA with anti-PR3 antibodies is characteristic of GPA, not EGPA. EGPA is associated with p-ANCA/anti-MPO in only 30-40% of cases.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Saddle nose deformity with nasal septal perforation is a clinical finding of GPA due to necrotizing granulomatous inflammation of nasal cartilage. EGPA causes nasal polyps, not saddle nose deformity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Serum cryoglobulins with hepatitis C are diagnostic of cryoglobulinemic vasculitis, not EGPA. The two conditions have entirely different pathogenic mechanisms.

questions.stem: A medical student is reviewing the classification of small-vessel vasculitides for an upcoming examination. She is trying to distinguish between ANCA-associated and immune complex-mediated vasculitides. Which of the following combinations correctly categorizes both disease groups?

choices.label: A
choices.text: ANCA-associated: GPA, EGPA, IgA vasculitis; Immune complex: MPA, cryoglobulinemia

choices.label: B
choices.text: ANCA-associated: GPA, EGPA, MPA; Immune complex: IgA vasculitis, cryoglobulinemia, anti-GBM disease

choices.label: C
choices.text: ANCA-associated: GPA, MPA, anti-GBM disease; Immune complex: EGPA, IgA vasculitis, cryoglobulinemia

choices.label: D
choices.text: ANCA-associated: GPA, MPA, cryoglobulinemia; Immune complex: EGPA, IgA vasculitis, anti-GBM disease

choices.label: E
choices.text: ANCA-associated: MPA, EGPA, anti-GBM disease; Immune complex: GPA, IgA vasculitis, cryoglobulinemia

explanation.summary: Small-vessel vasculitides are divided into two pathogenetically distinct subgroups: ANCA-associated (GPA, EGPA, MPA) and immune complex-mediated (IgA vasculitis, cryoglobulinemia, anti-GBM disease).
explanation.whyCorrect: ANCA-associated vasculitides include GPA (c-ANCA/anti-PR3), EGPA (p-ANCA/anti-MPO in ~50%), and MPA (p-ANCA/anti-MPO). Immune complex-mediated vasculitides include IgA vasculitis (IgA immune complexes), cryoglobulinemia (cryoglobulin immune complexes), and anti-GBM disease (anti-GBM antibody-mediated).

whyWrongByChoice.A: This incorrectly classifies IgA vasculitis as ANCA-associated and MPA as immune complex-mediated. IgA vasculitis is immune complex-mediated, and MPA is ANCA-associated (p-ANCA/anti-MPO).
whyWrongByChoice.C: This incorrectly classifies anti-GBM disease as ANCA-associated and EGPA as immune complex-mediated. Anti-GBM disease is immune complex/antibody-mediated, and EGPA is ANCA-associated.
whyWrongByChoice.D: This incorrectly classifies cryoglobulinemia as ANCA-associated and EGPA as immune complex-mediated. Cryoglobulinemia involves immune complex formation, and EGPA is associated with p-ANCA.
whyWrongByChoice.E: This incorrectly classifies GPA as immune complex-mediated and anti-GBM disease as ANCA-associated. GPA is the prototypical c-ANCA-associated vasculitis.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with a history of granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) presents with worsening sinusitis, hemoptysis, and rising serum creatinine. His c-ANCA and anti-PR3 levels have risen significantly from baseline. A renal biopsy is performed and shows crescentic glomerulonephritis. The treating rheumatologist decides to initiate aggressive immunosuppressive therapy. Which of the following treatment regimens is most appropriate for this patient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antiviral therapy with direct-acting agents targeting the underlying infection

choices.label: B
choices.text: Prednisone with azathioprine as the only immunosuppressive combination needed

choices.label: C
choices.text: High-dose intravenous immunoglobulin with aspirin to prevent vascular thrombosis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mepolizumab monotherapy targeting interleukin-5 to reduce eosinophilic inflammation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Corticosteroids combined with cyclophosphamide or rituximab, with plasmapheresis for severe disease

explanation.summary: GPA with active disease (worsening sinusitis, hemoptysis, rising creatinine, crescentic glomerulonephritis) requires aggressive immunosuppressive therapy with corticosteroids plus cyclophosphamide or rituximab. More severe disease may require plasmapheresis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The standard treatment for GPA is corticosteroids plus cyclophosphamide or rituximab. For more severe disease, plasmapheresis may be added. This patient has severe GPA with crescentic glomerulonephritis warranting aggressive therapy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antiviral therapy is the treatment approach for cryoglobulinemic vasculitis secondary to hepatitis C, not for GPA, which is an autoimmune ANCA-associated vasculitis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: IVIG with aspirin is the treatment for Kawasaki disease, a medium-vessel vasculitis in children. This combination is not used for GPA.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mepolizumab is approved for EGPA, not GPA. EGPA has eosinophilic inflammation responsive to IL-5 blockade, while GPA involves c-ANCA-mediated neutrophil activation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: While prednisone with azathioprine is used for PAN, GPA requires cyclophosphamide or rituximab due to the severity and ANCA-driven nature of the disease. Azathioprine alone is insufficient for induction therapy in GPA.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old female presents to the emergency department with a 5-day history of a new, severe, right-sided temporal headache that is unresponsive to acetaminophen. She also reports a 10-pound unintentional weight loss over the past 2 months and fatigue. She notes that her jaw becomes painful and fatigued after chewing for several minutes. On examination, there is tenderness to palpation over the right temporal region, and a thickened, nodular vessel is palpable. Laboratory studies reveal an ESR of 95 mm/hr and CRP of 8.2 mg/dL. A temporal artery biopsy is scheduled for the following day. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate action?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Withhold treatment until temporal artery biopsy results are available to confirm the diagnosis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Initiate high-dose corticosteroid therapy immediately without waiting for biopsy confirmation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Start low-dose aspirin and schedule outpatient follow-up for biopsy results in one week

choices.label: D
choices.text: Order MR angiography of the aortic arch and branches to evaluate for large-vessel involvement

choices.label: E
choices.text: Begin cyclophosphamide as first-line immunosuppressive therapy to prevent vision loss

explanation.summary: This patient has a classic presentation of giant cell arteritis. In patients with high clinical suspicion for GCA, high-dose corticosteroids should be started immediately, even before biopsy results are available, to prevent the most serious complication: permanent vision loss.
explanation.whyCorrect: When clinical suspicion for GCA is high, treatment with high-dose corticosteroids (such as prednisone) should be started immediately without waiting for biopsy results. Temporal artery biopsy may require time for processing and can show patchy involvement, and delaying treatment risks irreversible vision loss from optic neuropathy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Withholding treatment until biopsy confirmation is inappropriate because the biopsy results may take time, and arterial involvement can be patchy, making diagnosis difficult. Delaying treatment risks permanent blindness from ischemic optic neuropathy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Low-dose aspirin alone is insufficient for treating GCA. The standard treatment is high-dose corticosteroids. Aspirin does not address the underlying vascular inflammation that threatens vision, and delaying definitive therapy for outpatient follow-up is dangerous.
whyWrongByChoice.D: MR angiography is used in the diagnostic workup of Takayasu arteritis, not GCA. While GCA can involve the aorta, the immediate priority in this patient with visual symptoms at risk is to initiate corticosteroid therapy, not pursue additional imaging.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cyclophosphamide is not the first-line treatment for GCA. It is reserved as an alternative treatment option for patients who have contraindications or are nonresponsive to corticosteroids. High-dose corticosteroids are the standard initial therapy.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old female of Japanese descent presents with a 3-week history of malaise, low-grade fever, and pain in both arms that worsens when she carries grocery bags. She has lost 8 pounds over the past month. Her blood pressure is 135/88 mmHg in the right arm and 98/64 mmHg in the left arm. On examination, the left radial pulse is markedly diminished compared to the right. Laboratory studies show an ESR of 72 mm/hr and CRP of 5.4 mg/dL. Which of the following imaging findings would be most specific for this patient's underlying condition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hypoechoic halo surrounding the temporal artery lumen on duplex Doppler ultrasound

choices.label: B
choices.text: Focal aneurysmal dilation of the coronary arteries on echocardiography

choices.label: C
choices.text: Long, smooth, tapered stenosis with an undulating pattern on CT angiography

choices.label: D
choices.text: Beading pattern of alternating stenosis and dilation in medium-sized renal arteries

choices.label: E
choices.text: Concentric thickening of the ascending aorta with calcification on non-contrast CT

explanation.summary: This young Asian female with diminished upper extremity pulses, blood pressure discrepancy between arms, and systemic inflammatory symptoms has Takayasu arteritis. The characteristic imaging finding on CT angiography is long, smooth, tapered stenosis with an undulating pattern known as the 'macaroni sign.'
explanation.whyCorrect: Takayasu arteritis is diagnosed radiologically, often using MRA or CT angiography. The characteristic imaging finding is segments of long, smooth, tapered stenosis that may have an undulating pattern highly specific to Takayasu arteritis, known as the 'macaroni sign.' This is distinct from atherosclerotic stenosis, which is nonhomogeneous and involves shorter segments.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A hypoechoic halo surrounding the vessel lumen on duplex Doppler ultrasound is a characteristic finding of giant cell arteritis, not Takayasu arteritis. GCA primarily affects the temporal arteries in older patients, unlike this young patient with aortic branch involvement.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Focal aneurysmal dilation of the coronary arteries is a hallmark of Kawasaki disease, a medium-vessel vasculitis primarily affecting children. This finding is not associated with Takayasu arteritis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A beading pattern of alternating stenosis and dilation in medium-sized arteries is characteristic of fibromuscular dysplasia or polyarteritis nodosa, not Takayasu arteritis, which affects large vessels and shows long, smooth stenoses.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Concentric aortic thickening with calcification on non-contrast CT is a nonspecific finding that can be seen in atherosclerosis and other conditions. The specific diagnostic finding for Takayasu arteritis is the pattern of stenosis seen on contrast-enhanced angiographic imaging.

questions.stem: A 69-year-old female with a known history of polymyalgia rheumatica presents with a 2-day history of new-onset right temporal headache and an episode of transient monocular vision loss lasting 30 seconds in her right eye earlier today. She has been well controlled on low-dose prednisone for her PMR. On examination, she has tenderness over the right temporal artery. Laboratory studies show an ESR of 110 mm/hr. A temporal artery biopsy is performed and reveals a transmural inflammatory infiltrate with lymphocytes, macrophages, and multinucleated giant cells. Which of the following histologic features, when evaluated with a special stain, would further support the diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fibrinoid necrosis of the vessel wall demonstrated on hematoxylin and eosin staining

choices.label: B
choices.text: Focal fragmentation of the internal elastic membrane on elastic tissue stain

choices.label: C
choices.text: Concentric intimal fibrosis with onion-skin appearance on periodic acid-Schiff staining

choices.label: D
choices.text: Transmural neutrophilic infiltrate with leukocytoclasis on immunofluorescence staining

choices.label: E
choices.text: Caseating granulomas within the adventitia demonstrated on acid-fast bacilli staining

explanation.summary: This patient with PMR and new symptoms of GCA has a biopsy showing the classic granulomatous inflammatory infiltrate. An additional histologic feature of GCA is focal destruction of the internal elastic membrane, which requires an elastic tissue stain to evaluate.
explanation.whyCorrect: A characteristic histologic feature of GCA is focal fragmentation and destruction of the internal elastic membrane. This finding requires an elastic tissue stain (such as Verhoeff-Van Gieson stain) to properly evaluate and further supports the diagnosis of GCA when seen alongside the granulomatous inflammation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Fibrinoid necrosis is a hallmark of small-vessel and medium-vessel vasculitides such as polyarteritis nodosa and ANCA-associated vasculitis. GCA characteristically shows granulomatous inflammation with giant cells and elastic membrane destruction, not fibrinoid necrosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Concentric intimal fibrosis with an onion-skin appearance is characteristic of malignant hypertension or thrombotic microangiopathies affecting small arterioles, not the large-vessel granulomatous inflammation seen in GCA.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Transmural neutrophilic infiltrate with leukocytoclasis is the hallmark of leukocytoclastic vasculitis, a small-vessel vasculitis. GCA shows lymphocytes, macrophages, and giant cells, not a neutrophil-predominant infiltrate.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Caseating granulomas with acid-fast bacilli are diagnostic of tuberculous infection. GCA shows non-caseating granulomatous inflammation with giant cells and does not involve mycobacterial organisms.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old female presents with a 2-month history of progressive left arm fatigue and coolness, intermittent dizziness, and two episodes of near-syncope when turning her head to the left. She has also experienced unintentional weight loss of 6 kg. Her blood pressure is 142/90 mmHg in the right arm and 95/58 mmHg in the left arm. On auscultation, a bruit is heard over the left supraclavicular region. Laboratory studies reveal an ESR of 68 mm/hr. CT angiography demonstrates long, smooth stenosis of the left subclavian artery proximal to the origin of the left vertebral artery. Which of the following best explains her episodes of dizziness and near-syncope?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Carotid sinus hypersensitivity from inflammation of the carotid artery bifurcation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Orthostatic hypotension from adrenal insufficiency caused by chronic corticosteroid use

choices.label: C
choices.text: Retrograde flow in the vertebral artery due to proximal subclavian artery narrowing

choices.label: D
choices.text: Cardiac arrhythmia from myocardial inflammation secondary to coronary artery vasculitis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vertebrobasilar atherosclerotic disease from accelerated atherosclerosis in young females

explanation.summary: This patient has Takayasu arteritis complicated by subclavian steal syndrome. Proximal narrowing or occlusion of the subclavian artery leads to retrograde blood flow in the vertebral artery (blood flows away from the brain), causing syncope, dizziness, and neurologic deficits.
explanation.whyCorrect: Subclavian steal syndrome is a complication of Takayasu arteritis caused by proximal narrowing or occlusion of the subclavian artery. This leads to retrograde blood flow in the vertebral artery—blood travels away from the brain instead of toward it—resulting in posterior circulation ischemia manifested as syncope, dizziness, and neurologic deficits.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Carotid sinus hypersensitivity causes reflex bradycardia and hypotension from mechanical pressure on the carotid sinus and is typically seen in elderly patients. It does not explain the subclavian bruit, blood pressure discrepancy, or arm symptoms in this patient.
whyWrongByChoice.B: This patient has not been described as being on corticosteroids, so adrenal insufficiency from chronic steroid use is not applicable. Her dizziness is positional and related to vertebral artery flow reversal, not orthostatic hypotension.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Coronary artery vasculitis causing arrhythmia is not a typical complication of Takayasu arteritis. The clinical findings of blood pressure discrepancy, subclavian bruit, and arm claudication point to subclavian steal syndrome as the cause of her neurologic symptoms.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vertebrobasilar atherosclerosis typically affects older patients with traditional cardiovascular risk factors. This young female has an inflammatory large-vessel vasculitis causing stenosis, not accelerated atherosclerosis.

questions.stem: A 76-year-old female presents with bilateral shoulder and hip stiffness that is worst in the morning and improves with activity over the course of 1-2 hours. She has had these symptoms for 3 months and also reports fatigue and a 5-pound weight loss. She denies headache, jaw pain, or visual changes. Physical examination reveals limited active range of motion of both shoulders but full passive range of motion. There is no muscle weakness or tenderness. Laboratory studies show an ESR of 88 mm/hr, CRP of 6.1 mg/dL, and normal creatine kinase levels. Which of the following conditions is she at greatest risk of developing?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Dermatomyositis with proximal muscle weakness and characteristic heliotrope rash

choices.label: B
choices.text: Rheumatoid arthritis with symmetric small joint involvement and positive rheumatoid factor

choices.label: C
choices.text: Giant cell arteritis with headache, jaw claudication, and risk of permanent vision loss

choices.label: D
choices.text: Systemic lupus erythematosus with malar rash, arthritis, and nephritis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Polyarteritis nodosa with renal artery aneurysms and mesenteric ischemia

explanation.summary: This patient has polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR), characterized by bilateral shoulder and hip stiffness, elevated inflammatory markers, and normal creatine kinase. PMR has a strong association with giant cell arteritis (GCA)—up to 15% of PMR patients develop GCA, making her at greatest risk for this condition.
explanation.whyCorrect: PMR has a strong association with GCA. Up to half of GCA patients have PMR, and 15% of PMR patients have GCA. Symptoms of PMR and GCA can occur concurrently or independently. Since this patient has established PMR, she is at greatest risk of developing GCA with its potential complications including headache, jaw claudication, and permanent vision loss.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Dermatomyositis causes proximal muscle weakness with elevated creatine kinase levels and characteristic skin findings. This patient has normal CK and no muscle weakness, and PMR is now understood to involve inflammation of proximal joint bursae and tendons, not the muscles themselves.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Rheumatoid arthritis typically involves symmetric small joint synovitis with erosive changes. PMR causes proximal joint bursitis and tenosynovitis, and its strongest disease association is with GCA, not rheumatoid arthritis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Systemic lupus erythematosus typically presents in younger females with multi-system involvement. There is no established association between PMR and SLE, unlike the well-documented association between PMR and GCA.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Polyarteritis nodosa is a medium-vessel vasculitis without an established association with PMR. The strong epidemiologic and pathophysiologic link between PMR and GCA makes GCA the condition this patient is most at risk for developing.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old female from South Korea presents with a 6-week history of fatigue, night sweats, and diffuse myalgias. Over the past week, she has noticed that her left hand becomes pale and cold when she exercises. Her blood pressure is 128/82 mmHg in the right arm and 86/54 mmHg in the left arm. The left radial pulse is absent. Laboratory studies reveal elevated ESR and CRP. CT angiography confirms the suspected diagnosis. Which of the following additional complications should be specifically monitored for in this patient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Permanent blindness from anterior ischemic optic neuropathy caused by ophthalmic artery occlusion

choices.label: B
choices.text: Renovascular hypertension from renal artery involvement and activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system

choices.label: C
choices.text: Pulmonary hemorrhage from capillaritis and immune complex deposition in the alveolar capillaries

choices.label: D
choices.text: Glomerulonephritis from circulating immune complexes depositing in the glomerular basement membrane

choices.label: E
choices.text: Mononeuritis multiplex from vasa nervorum inflammation causing asymmetric peripheral nerve damage

explanation.summary: This patient has Takayasu arteritis. An important complication is vasculitis of the renal arteries or the aorta proximal to the renal arteries, causing renovascular (secondary) hypertension from reduced renal arterial flow and consequent activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system.
explanation.whyCorrect: Takayasu arteritis can involve the renal arteries or the aorta proximal to the renal arteries. This reduces renal arterial flow and activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, leading to renovascular (secondary) hypertension. This is a specific and important complication that should be monitored for in patients with Takayasu arteritis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Permanent blindness from anterior ischemic optic neuropathy is the most serious complication of giant cell arteritis, not Takayasu arteritis. While blindness can occur in Takayasu arteritis, the ophthalmic artery occlusion mechanism described here is characteristic of GCA.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pulmonary hemorrhage from capillaritis is a complication of small-vessel vasculitides such as granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) and microscopic polyangiitis, not large-vessel vasculitis like Takayasu arteritis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Glomerulonephritis from immune complex deposition is associated with small-vessel vasculitides and conditions like lupus nephritis, not Takayasu arteritis. Renal involvement in Takayasu arteritis occurs through large-vessel stenosis, not glomerular immune complex deposition.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Mononeuritis multiplex from vasa nervorum inflammation is characteristic of medium-vessel vasculitides such as polyarteritis nodosa, not the large-vessel vasculitis seen in Takayasu arteritis.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old male presents to his primary care physician with a 1-week history of right-sided temporal headache and pain in his jaw when chewing steak. He also reports that he has had difficulty combing his hair because his scalp is tender. He denies visual changes. His ESR is 92 mm/hr and CRP is 7.8 mg/dL. A duplex Doppler ultrasound of the temporal arteries is performed. Which of the following ultrasound findings would be most supportive of the suspected diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Complete absence of flow signal in the temporal artery suggesting total occlusion

choices.label: B
choices.text: Calcified intimal plaques with turbulent flow patterns suggesting atherosclerotic disease

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased temporal artery diameter with a hypoechoic smooth halo surrounding the lumen

choices.label: D
choices.text: Irregular aneurysmal dilation of the temporal artery with oscillating intraluminal thrombus

choices.label: E
choices.text: Normal-appearing temporal arteries with preserved laminar flow on color Doppler imaging

explanation.summary: This patient has a classic presentation of GCA. On duplex Doppler ultrasound, the characteristic finding is increased diameter of the temporal artery with a hypoechoic smooth halo surrounding the lumen, known as the 'halo effect,' which represents the thickened arterial wall from vascular inflammation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Duplex Doppler ultrasound can support the diagnosis of GCA with a sensitivity of 87% and specificity of 96%. The characteristic finding is increased diameter of the temporal artery with hypoechoic smooth muscle surrounding the lumen, producing a 'halo effect.' The halo represents the thickened arterial wall resulting from vascular inflammation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Complete absence of flow could occur in advanced GCA with total occlusion but is not the characteristic diagnostic finding. The hallmark ultrasound finding is the hypoechoic halo sign, which represents the inflammatory thickening of the arterial wall.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Calcified intimal plaques with turbulent flow are findings of atherosclerotic disease, not vasculitis. Atherosclerotic changes involve nonhomogeneous, shorter segment involvement, whereas GCA shows a smooth, circumferential hypoechoic halo.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Irregular aneurysmal dilation with intraluminal thrombus is not a typical finding in GCA. GCA characteristically causes arterial wall thickening and luminal narrowing from the inflammatory infiltrate and subsequent fibrosis, not aneurysmal dilation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Normal-appearing temporal arteries would not support the diagnosis. While GCA can involve the temporal artery in a patchy fashion, the question asks for findings supportive of the diagnosis, and normal ultrasound would not fulfill this criterion.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old female with recently diagnosed giant cell arteritis has been on high-dose prednisone for 4 weeks with significant improvement in her headache and jaw claudication. However, she has developed steroid-related side effects including significant weight gain, hyperglycemia, and insomnia. Her physician wants to transition her to a steroid-sparing agent. Which of the following medications would be most appropriate as an alternative therapy for this patient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Adalimumab, a monoclonal antibody that binds TNF-alpha and decreases pro-inflammatory cascades

choices.label: B
choices.text: Methotrexate, a folate antagonist that inhibits dihydrofolate reductase and suppresses lymphocyte proliferation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Tocilizumab, an IL-6 receptor antagonist that modulates the inflammatory response in vasculitis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Rituximab, an anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody that depletes B lymphocytes from the circulation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Azathioprine, a purine analog that inhibits nucleotide synthesis and reduces immune cell proliferation

explanation.summary: In GCA patients facing severe adverse effects of corticosteroid use, IL-6 antagonists such as tocilizumab are used as steroid-sparing agents.
explanation.whyCorrect: Tocilizumab is an IL-6 receptor antagonist specifically indicated for GCA patients who experience severe adverse effects from corticosteroid use. It serves as a steroid-sparing agent that allows reduction of corticosteroid dosing while maintaining disease control.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Adalimumab, a TNF-alpha inhibitor, is used in the treatment of Takayasu arteritis with corticosteroids, not as the steroid-sparing agent of choice for GCA. The source material specifically identifies tocilizumab (an IL-6 antagonist) for GCA patients with corticosteroid adverse effects.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Methotrexate is used as a steroid-sparing agent in various rheumatic conditions, but it is not identified as the recommended alternative for GCA patients with corticosteroid side effects. Tocilizumab is the specifically recommended IL-6 antagonist for this purpose.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Rituximab is an anti-CD20 antibody used in ANCA-associated vasculitis and certain autoimmune conditions. It is not the recommended steroid-sparing agent for GCA.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Azathioprine is a general immunosuppressant used in various autoimmune conditions but is not the specifically recommended steroid-sparing therapy for GCA. Tocilizumab is the targeted biologic agent recommended for this indication.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old female presents with a 4-week history of low-grade fever, malaise, and bilateral arm pain that worsens with exertion. She works as a personal trainer and has noticed difficulty lifting weights overhead. On examination, her blood pressure is 150/95 mmHg in both legs but 105/68 mmHg in the right arm and 100/62 mmHg in the left arm. Both radial pulses are weak. Auscultation reveals a bruit over the abdominal aorta. Laboratory studies show ESR of 80 mm/hr. CT angiography reveals long, smooth stenosis of both subclavian arteries and the infrarenal aorta. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial pharmacologic treatment?

choices.label: A
choices.text: High-dose intravenous immunoglobulin to modulate the inflammatory immune response

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cyclophosphamide monotherapy as the primary immunosuppressive agent for large-vessel vasculitis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Tocilizumab monotherapy as the preferred IL-6 receptor antagonist for aortic arch vasculitis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Adalimumab combined with corticosteroids to inhibit TNF-alpha and reduce vascular inflammation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Colchicine and low-dose aspirin to reduce neutrophil-mediated inflammation and prevent thrombosis

explanation.summary: This patient has Takayasu arteritis based on her age, sex, bilateral subclavian and aortic stenosis, diminished upper extremity pulses, and elevated inflammatory markers. The treatment for Takayasu arteritis is adalimumab (a TNF-alpha inhibitor) combined with corticosteroids.
explanation.whyCorrect: The treatment for Takayasu arteritis is adalimumab with corticosteroids such as prednisone. Adalimumab is a monoclonal antibody that binds to TNF-alpha, decreasing the activation of pro-inflammatory cascades activated by cytokine release, thereby reducing the vascular inflammation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Intravenous immunoglobulin is used in conditions such as Kawasaki disease and certain autoimmune neuropathies. It is not the standard treatment for Takayasu arteritis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cyclophosphamide is not used routinely for large-vessel vasculitis. It may be used as an alternative treatment option when patients have contraindications or are nonresponsive to corticosteroids, but it is not the first-line treatment.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Tocilizumab (an IL-6 antagonist) is used as a steroid-sparing agent in GCA, not as the primary treatment for Takayasu arteritis. The standard treatment for Takayasu arteritis is adalimumab combined with corticosteroids.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Colchicine and aspirin are not the standard treatment for Takayasu arteritis. Colchicine is used for gout and pericarditis, and aspirin alone does not adequately address the large-vessel vascular inflammation in Takayasu arteritis.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old female presents to the emergency department with sudden painless vision loss in her left eye that began 2 hours ago. She reports a 3-week history of left temporal headache and jaw fatigue while eating. Her ESR is 105 mm/hr. She is started on high-dose corticosteroids and a temporal artery biopsy is performed. The biopsy reveals transmural inflammation with lymphocytes and macrophages, but no giant cells are identified. Which of the following statements best explains the significance of these biopsy findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The absence of giant cells rules out the diagnosis of giant cell arteritis and an alternative diagnosis should be pursued

choices.label: B
choices.text: The biopsy is consistent with Takayasu arteritis since giant cells are only found in younger patients

choices.label: C
choices.text: Giant cells are present in approximately 75% of GCA cases and their absence does not exclude the diagnosis

choices.label: D
choices.text: The corticosteroid treatment likely eliminated all giant cells before the biopsy could be performed

choices.label: E
choices.text: The biopsy specimen was inadequate and a repeat biopsy from the contralateral temporal artery is mandatory

explanation.summary: Giant cells are found in approximately 75% of GCA biopsies. Since vessel involvement can be patchy, the presence of giant cells is not required for diagnosis despite the disease's name. The transmural inflammatory infiltrate with lymphocytes and macrophages is still consistent with GCA.
explanation.whyCorrect: The classic histologic picture of GCA includes a transmural inflammatory infiltrate of lymphocytes, macrophages, and in approximately 75% of cases, multinucleated giant cells. Because vessel involvement can be patchy, the presence of giant cells is not required for diagnosis. The findings of transmural inflammation with lymphocytes and macrophages in a patient with a classic clinical presentation remain consistent with GCA.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The absence of giant cells does not rule out GCA. Giant cells are present in only about 75% of cases, and their absence does not exclude the diagnosis, especially when the clinical presentation and other histologic findings are consistent with GCA.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Takayasu arteritis and GCA have very similar histologic appearances and both can show giant cells. The diseases are differentiated by clinical signs, symptoms, and patient demographics, not by the presence or absence of giant cells on biopsy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: While corticosteroids can alter biopsy findings over time, the biopsy was performed promptly in this case. The more relevant explanation is that giant cells are only present in approximately 75% of GCA biopsies, making their absence an expected finding in a quarter of cases.
whyWrongByChoice.E: While GCA can be patchy and a contralateral biopsy may sometimes be considered, the current biopsy showing transmural inflammation with lymphocytes and macrophages in the context of a highly suggestive clinical presentation is sufficient to support the diagnosis.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old female college student presents with a 6-week history of progressive fatigue, low-grade fevers, and aching in both arms. She has noticed that her left arm becomes numb and pale when she raises it above her head during volleyball practice. On examination, her left radial pulse is absent, and a bruit is heard over the left subclavian artery. Her blood pressure is 140/92 mmHg in the right arm and undetectable in the left arm. Laboratory studies show an ESR of 75 mm/hr and a CRP of 6.2 mg/dL. The patient asks whether a tissue biopsy will be needed for diagnosis. Which of the following is the most appropriate response regarding the diagnostic approach?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A temporal artery biopsy is required to differentiate this condition from giant cell arteritis

choices.label: B
choices.text: An artery biopsy is typically not used or needed; diagnosis is made radiologically with MRA or CT angiography

choices.label: C
choices.text: A subclavian artery biopsy is the gold standard diagnostic test and should be performed immediately

choices.label: D
choices.text: A skin punch biopsy of the affected arm will reveal the characteristic histologic features of this disease

choices.label: E
choices.text: An endomyocardial biopsy is indicated to evaluate for cardiac involvement before initiating therapy

explanation.summary: This patient has Takayasu arteritis. Unlike GCA, an artery biopsy is typically not used or needed for diagnosis of Takayasu arteritis. The diagnosis is made radiologically, often using MRA or CT angiography.
explanation.whyCorrect: Unlike GCA, which requires temporal artery biopsy for definitive diagnosis, Takayasu arteritis is diagnosed radiologically using MRA or CT angiography. Artery biopsy is typically not used or needed. Imaging findings include segments of long, smooth, tapered stenosis which may show the characteristic 'macaroni sign.'

whyWrongByChoice.A: Temporal artery biopsy is the diagnostic test for GCA, not Takayasu arteritis. The two diseases are differentiated by clinical presentation and patient demographics—GCA affects patients over 50 while Takayasu affects younger patients. This young patient's clinical features clearly point to Takayasu arteritis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Subclavian artery biopsy is not the standard diagnostic approach for Takayasu arteritis. Biopsy of large arteries carries significant procedural risks, and the diagnosis can be reliably made with non-invasive radiologic imaging such as MRA or CT angiography.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Skin punch biopsy would not reveal the vascular histologic changes of Takayasu arteritis, which involves the aorta and its primary branches. The diagnosis is made through vascular imaging, not skin biopsy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Endomyocardial biopsy is used for diagnosing cardiac conditions such as myocarditis or transplant rejection, not Takayasu arteritis. While Takayasu can affect the aorta, its diagnosis relies on vascular imaging rather than cardiac tissue sampling.

questions.stem: A 73-year-old female with a 4-month history of polymyalgia rheumatica controlled on low-dose prednisone presents with a new right-sided temporal headache, malaise, and transient blurring of vision in her right eye. Her ESR is 98 mm/hr and CRP is 9.1 mg/dL. She is started on high-dose prednisone, and a temporal artery biopsy confirms GCA with transmural granulomatous inflammation, multinucleated giant cells, and luminal narrowing. Which of the following best describes the mechanism by which this patient's most feared complication develops?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Embolic occlusion of the central retinal artery from thrombus formation within the inflamed temporal artery

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ischemic injury to the optic nerve from vasculitic occlusion of branches of the ophthalmic artery

choices.label: C
choices.text: Direct granulomatous infiltration of the optic nerve by inflammatory cells extending from the temporal artery

choices.label: D
choices.text: Compression of the optic chiasm from edema and inflammation spreading to the intracranial compartment

choices.label: E
choices.text: Retinal detachment caused by choroidal vasculitis and disruption of the retinal pigment epithelium

explanation.summary: The most serious complication of GCA is permanent vision loss, most commonly caused by optic neuropathy. Ischemia from the vasculitis causes occlusion of the posterior circulation to the optic nerve, specifically branches of the ophthalmic artery arising from the internal carotid artery, leading to nerve injury and death.
